c: Lakeview Conference Center, a venue that hosts corporate meetings, weddings and fundraisers
j: client, the director of a nonprofit
s: The director of a local nonprofit wants to host an annual fundraising dinner at Lakeview for 250 guests in six weeks. The budget is $22,000, and the director wants a keynote speaker, a silent auction and a plated dinner. The venue is booked for a wedding the same weekend, but can offer Friday night or Sunday afternoon.
The director (judge) is anxious about cost and timing and wants to know whether the event is realistic. You must explain the plan, the choices on date and menu, and how to stay within the budget.
You have 7 minutes to present your event plan, compare options with pros and cons, and recommend a decision.
f: Guests: 250; budget: $22,000
Plated dinner: $48 a person; buffet: $34 a person; dessert reception: $18 a person
Venue fee: $3,500 Friday evening, $2,800 Sunday afternoon
Audio and projector rental: $1,200; keynote speaker fee: $2,500
Past events raised $38,000 at 200 guests
d: present your event plan to the client
n: Builds a budget and shows that a plated dinner for 250 ($12,000) plus the venue and speaker nearly consumes the budget
Compares Friday night, Sunday afternoon, plated and buffet options with pros and cons
Recommends a specific package that fits $22,000, such as a buffet or a reception
Lays out a timeline of tasks from invitations to follow-up
Includes risk planning for weather, no-shows and equipment
Explains how the venue will measure success and keep the client informed
q: How can we still raise more money if we cut the dinner budget?
What happens if only 180 guests come?
Which part of the plan worries you most?

s: Harborview's online review score fell from 4.4 to 3.8 stars in three months. Common complaints include long check-in lines, slow responses to room requests and noise from a nearby construction site. A regional conference next month will bring 90 guests, so the general manager wants fast improvements.

The general manager (judge) can spend up to $15,000 and wants you to identify the root causes, compare options such as adding staff at peak times, a mobile check-in system, and noise-reduction measures, and recommend a plan.
You have 7 minutes to explain your analysis and recommendation.
f: Review score: 3.8 stars (down from 4.4)
Check-in wait at peak (3-6 p.m.): average 11 minutes
Mobile check-in system: $9,000; extra desk staff at peak for a month: $3,200; earplugs, white noise machines and room moves: $2,400
Construction continues for another 8 weeks, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Conference group: 90 guests arriving on a Thursday afternoon
n: Separates the three complaints and identifies the likely causes
Compares options with costs, speed and effect on guests
Recommends a package within $15,000, such as extra staff at peak, noise measures and a small guest gesture
Plans specifically for the conference group's arrival
Describes how to respond to the online reviews
Sets measures such as wait times and review score by month
q: Which problem do you fix first and why?
Is mobile check-in worth $9,000 for a hotel this size?
How do we handle guests already angry about the noise?

c: Palm Cove Resort, a beach resort that is slow in the fall
s: Palm Cove Resort runs at 85 percent occupancy in summer but only 38 percent in October and November. The marketing director wants to fill rooms in the slow season without cutting room rates so deeply that the brand suffers. Ideas include a package for corporate retreats, a weekday family deal, and partnerships with a local wedding planner.
The marketing director (judge) has a promotion budget of $18,000. You must analyze the options, recommend what to do, and explain how to sell the plan to potential customers.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis.
f: Rooms: 160; average room rate: $210 in summer, $145 in fall
October-November occupancy: 38%, target 55%
Corporate retreat package: 40 rooms for 2 nights at $130 a night, meeting rooms included
Weekday family deal: 3 nights for the price of 2
Promotion budget: $18,000
n: Defines target markets for each option
Calculates the value of a goal: 17% more occupancy is about 27 rooms a night
Compares options with revenue, cost and brand effects
Recommends a mix and a budget for ads, partnerships and sales calls
Describes how to sell to corporate buyers and families differently
Sets measures such as bookings by package and revenue per available room
q: Won't discounts train guests to wait for low prices?
How would you reach corporate buyers with a small budget?
What would you do if the retreat package fills but the family deal doesn't?

c: Bayside Bistro, a restaurant that also hosts private parties
s: Bayside Bistro hosts about 40 private parties a year in a back room that seats 60. The owner thinks the parties are profitable but is not sure, because the restaurant also has to turn away regular dinner customers when the back room is closed for an event. Food costs, staffing and cleaning vary, and the owner is considering raising the room fee, adding a minimum spend, or stopping parties on busy Friday nights.
The owner (judge) wants you to analyze the numbers and recommend pricing and policy changes to make the private party business more profitable.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis and recommendation.
f: Average private party: 45 guests; food and drink revenue $2,850; room fee $300
Direct costs: food and drink 34% of sales; staff $520; cleaning and setup $140
On Friday nights, a regular dinner service in the same room earns about $3,100 in sales at a 32% cost of goods
Parties per year: 40, of which 14 are on Fridays
Owner wants a minimum profit of at least $900 per party
n: Calculates profit per party: $3,150 revenue less about $1,629 in direct costs leaves roughly $1,520
Compares it with the Friday regular-service alternative
Compares raising the room fee, a minimum spend, or stopping Friday parties, with pros and cons
Recommends a policy and checks it against the $900 target
Considers how customers will react to the change
Explains how to track profit by event going forward
q: If Friday dinners earn more, why would I ever book a Friday party?
How would customers react to a minimum spend?
What costs did you leave out?

c: Alpine Ski Lodge, a lodge with 80 rooms and a restaurant
s: Alpine Ski Lodge keeps guest reservations on paper and in three different spreadsheets. Last weekend, the lodge double-booked six rooms and lost the contact information of a group of 30 guests. The general manager is considering buying a property management system, using a cloud booking tool, or hiring a part-time data clerk.

The general manager (judge) wants to fix the problem before the holiday season, which begins in six weeks. The lodge has a budget of $12,000 for a solution. You need to explain how the problems are affecting the business and recommend a solution.
You have 7 minutes to present your plan.
f: Double bookings last weekend: 6 rooms; estimated cost in refunds and goodwill: $2,100
Property management system: $9,500 setup plus $180 a month
Cloud booking tool: $2,400 a year; limited reporting
Part-time data clerk: $1,600 a month
Holiday bookings so far: 61 reservations
n: Explains how poor information management leads to double bookings and lost guest data
Compares the three options with cost, speed and benefits
Considers data security and privacy of guest information
Recommends a plan that is working before the holiday season
Describes staff training and a backup plan
Sets measures, such as zero double bookings and faster check-in
q: Can we get something working in six weeks?
How would we protect our guests' payment information?
Is a system worth $9,500 for a lodge this size?
